Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

zuarrow 0.0.0.9000

  • Initial CRAN submission.

Handles

  • arrow_schema() makes a schema handle from an Arrow format string, from an R object, or from any schema, array or stream handle, and format() and print() show Arrow’s type notation.
  • Handles share the ‘nanoarrow’ package’s layout and inherit from its classes, so handles cross between the two packages without conversion.
  • arrow_validate() runs the bundled ‘nanoarrow’ C library’s validation at "minimal", "default" or "full"; "full" also checks that every string is valid UTF-8.
  • arrow_equal() compares two schemas, arrays or streams, and says why they differ.
  • arrow_metadata() and arrow_metadata<- read and write schema metadata, keeping binary values as raw vectors.
  • zuarrow_info() reports the versions zuarrow is built from.
  • Every error inherits from zuarrow_error, and the lossy warning from zuarrow_warning.

Converting to and from R

  • arrow_to_r() converts an array to an R vector and a stream or struct array to a data frame; as.data.frame() and as.vector() do the same, and arrow_next() reads one batch.
  • A conversion is exact or it fails: lossy = "error", the default everywhere, raises zuarrow_lossy_error naming the column, the row and the package that would read it exactly. lossy = "character" gives the values’ exact text, "warn" and "allow" the nearest R type.
  • to names the R type a column must become.
  • Conversion in both directions reads and writes typed buffers in one loop wherever a column has no dictionary or run-end encoding, so most types convert as fast as with nanoarrow or faster, with every exactness check kept.
  • copy = FALSE defers string columns in arrow_to_r(), arrow_next(), arrow_read() and as.data.frame(). Each becomes a character vector that creates its R strings on first use, which is most of the cost of a string column. Values are checked during the conversion either way, so the errors are the same. The default, copy = TRUE, creates every value at once.
  • arrow_array() and arrow_stream() build arrays and streams from R vectors and data frames, checking every value against a given schema. The exact text that lossy = "character" returns is written back as the type its arrow_type attribute names.
  • arrow_types() lists the built-in type table.

Nested types, dictionaries and the registry

  • Structs convert to nested data frames, lists of every kind to list columns, fixed-size lists to list columns or, with arrow_matrix(), to matrices, and maps to lists of key/value data frames. Each converts back.
  • Factors convert to and from dictionary<int32, utf8>, ordered factors included; a stream’s batches read as the union of their levels. Other dictionaries and run-end encoded arrays decode to their values.
  • Extension types keep their name and metadata as attributes and are restored on export; arrow.bool8 reads as logical. Field metadata round-trips through the arrow_field_metadata attribute.
  • arrow_register(), arrow_unregister() and arrow_registry() let a package make a lossy type exact with its own R class, by format string, prefix pattern or extension name, in both directions.

The IPC file and stream formats

  • arrow_read() reads the Arrow IPC file format (.arrow, Feather version 2) and stream format (.arrows) from a path, a raw vector or a connection, eagerly into a data frame or lazily as a stream, with column selection.
  • LZ4 and zstd bodies are decompressed through ‘zukomp’, so a compressed file opens everywhere; dictionary batches and deltas are applied, and the binary-view, string-view, list-view and run-end-encoded layouts decode.
  • Every message is verified and checked against arrow_limits() before it is used, and every batch passes full validation, so hostile input is a zuarrow_format_error or zuarrow_limit_error. Big-endian input is refused.
  • Full validation also checks that every binary or string view points inside its buffers, which the bundled C library does not.
  • arrow_write() writes data frames, struct arrays and streams as the Arrow IPC file or stream format, to a path, a connection or a raw vector, in record batches of batch rows.
  • Factors are written as dictionaries, one dictionary batch before the first record batch, or as strings with dictionary = FALSE; schema and field metadata and extension names are kept.
  • compression = "lz4" or "zstd" compresses each buffer through ‘zukomp’, at the codec’s own level; the default is uncompressed, so every reader opens the output.
  • The output is deterministic: the same input gives the same bytes, with no timestamps and every padding byte zeroed.

Fixes

  • arrow_metadata<- raises zuarrow_type_error for a key that is not valid UTF-8 or a value that is not raw. Before, it raised a plain zuarrow_error.

  • A list column of data frames keeps every row of every element; before, its offsets counted columns, not rows, and rows were dropped (#31).

  • Writing a string that is not valid UTF-8, or that is marked as "bytes", is a zuarrow_type_error naming the row. Before, it built an invalid array or raised an unclassed error. Column names are checked the same way (#35).

  • Writing a factor whose code names no level, or whose levels are not strings, is a zuarrow_type_error naming the row, with or without a dictionary (#36).

  • arrow_write() leaves an array it writes usable. Before, it released the caller’s array, so it could not be read or written again (#40).

  • arrow_array() and arrow_stream() no longer set an attribute on the schema handle they are given (#53).

  • Every character column switches to large_utf8 past 2^31 - 1 bytes, including data frame and list columns, and arrow_schema() reports the switch (#52).

  • A map column converts back to a map. A list with the arrow_keys_sorted attribute is written as map, and a map schema accepts a list of key/value data frames. A null key is a zuarrow_type_error (#41).

  • arrow_equal() compares arrays value by value, as the design says: the bytes under a null slot and the array offset no longer count, and a dictionary or run-end encoded array compares by its decoded values (#64).

  • A dictionary index outside its dictionary is a zuarrow_format_error for every dictionary, not only for factors. Before, a dictionary of numbers read past its end (#50).

  • A factor level with an embedded NUL is cut at the NUL under lossy = "warn" or "allow", as a plain string is, and the lossy error names the dictionary column’s format. Before, it raised an unclassed error (#37).

  • With copy = FALSE, strings inside list elements are copied, as the design says, rather than each element deferring and keeping every batch alive (#55).

  • A decimal with a negative scale round-trips through its text form: the text needs the scale’s trailing zeros, and zero reads as "0" (#54).

  • Registered to handlers apply to the fields of nested data frames at any depth, as documented, and a handled field under a null struct row is NA. Before, only top-level columns used them (#42).

  • An inexact registration may not replace the exact conversion of second and millisecond timestamps, fixed_size_list or the list views (#78).

  • A list column with NULL elements writes to a fixed_size_list, whose null rows still hold their width of child values. Before, it was a zuarrow_type_error, so such a column read from Arrow could not be written back (found by the #48 oracle).

  • arrow_write() computes a null count the producer left unknown (-1) before it writes the batch. Before, the file it wrote could not be read back (#34).

  • arrow_read() refuses a field name or metadata key that holds a NUL or is not valid UTF-8 with a zuarrow_format_error, and so do arrow_metadata() and arrow_to_r() for such a schema. Before, a NUL raised an unclassed error, a NUL in a name cut it short, and invalid bytes became a string marked UTF-8 (#38).

  • A compression level outside the codec’s range, and any codec failure while writing, is a zuarrow_codec_error. Before, it was an unclassed zuarrow_error (#39).

  • arrow_read() finds the size of a file through 64-bit offsets, so a file over 2 GiB opens on Windows (#51).

  • arrow_read() reads a raw vector in place rather than copying it, except with lazy = TRUE, whose handle keeps its own copy (#57).

  • arrow_read() refuses a file whose footer’s copy of the schema differs from its schema message with a zuarrow_format_error. Before, it read the message’s copy, where libarrow reads the footer’s (#33).

  • arrow_read(lazy = TRUE) with to, lossy or copy set is a zuarrow_type_error. Before, it ignored them silently (#78).

  • An unknown lossy, level, format or compression is a zuarrow_type_error, so it inherits from zuarrow_error like every other error. Before, match.arg() raised an unclassed error. The value must now match a choice exactly (#32).

  • arrow_write() raises zuarrow_io_error when it cannot open or write to a path or a connection, and the message keeps the cause, as arrow_read() does. Before, a connection raised unclassed errors and a path lost the cause (#76).

  • as.vector() with a mode other than "any", and as.data.frame() with row.names, are a zuarrow_type_error. Before, both were ignored silently. optional is documented as ignored (#77).

  • The lossy error and warning for a field of a nested data frame that is converted for a registered handler name its path, such as s$b, in the message and in column. Before, they named b alone (#42).

  • Error messages follow one style: “must” for a requirement and “can’t” for what is impossible, one idea per sentence (#80).

  • A list column of functions, environments or calls is a zuarrow_type_error. Before, arrow_schema(list(sum)) recursed until the C stack overflowed (#82).
